lines.text: You walked a long way to get here. Almost everyone here walked.
The cities you left behind are still standing. This one isn't.
Hey. You're one of the ones who came in this week, aren't you? It shows on your face.
Welcome. I live in that house over there, the one that still has a roof.
Look around. This was a wall. Now it's rubble, and rubble keeps nobody outside.

lines.frame: People came up from the big city asking how we were getting on. This is how it was put to them:

lines.text: That's why we came back, and that's why nobody sleeps properly. We're home and the home is wide open.
Today is different, though. A man came from the capital, with letters from the king, and called everyone together by the wall.
Nobody's quite sure who he is. I know he rode out before dawn, alone, to see the size of the damage before he opened his mouth.
That already tells me more than a speech would.
Come on. Not in those road clothes, though. Go inside, find something decent, and we'll walk down together.
Better. Now you look like you came to stay, not like you came to look.
Come on. Everyone's down there already.
The man from the capital climbed onto a stone where everyone could see him. He waited for the noise to die down.
— Some of you got here this week. Others were born here, in the middle of it.
— I went out at night to see the wall, and came back in by the same gate I left by. Before I said a word to anyone. I know the size of what I am asking.

lines.frame: Then he said it, and he said it like someone who had already counted the stones one by one:
He told them what he had come back with, and what the people answered:

lines.text: Then he was quiet for a while. It wasn't a pause for effect; it was something else.

lines.frame: The neighbour beside you whispered that he has been praying like that since before he got here:

lines.text: — Each of you takes the stretch nearest your own house.
Beside you, the same neighbour muttered the rest under his breath: nobody hauls stone for a wall that doesn't cover their own door.
— The stone is in the rubble. It's the same stone that fell. Start today.
And that was it. Nobody clapped. People went — and all of them went.
My father mixed resin with oil and sold it in small jars. I know the smell of everything that was ever good on this street.
Now I know the weight of a burnt stone. I learned it in two days, and I'd rather not have.
My sister sleeps at her father-in-law's, the other side of the valley. There's no door here that shuts, and what has no door isn't a house.

lines.text: I didn't enjoy hearing it. I couldn't find a word of it to argue with either.
Shallum. Those two on the mortar are my daughters. Don't pull that face: they lay better than I do, and I've been laying for twenty years.
The arithmetic here is short and nobody likes it. Every person on top of the wall at night is a person off the stone during the day.
And if there's nobody up there, you spend the day lifting what they throw down at night. There's no pretty way out. There's a choice.

lines.frame: What was said after that was set down like this:

lines.text: It was easier said than done. But we said it, and I was there.
Baruch. I took that stretch over there, the one facing the open ground.
Everyone picks the piece in front of their own house. Somebody has to take the one you can see from far off.
There's room on my side, if you want it. I won't pretend it's the same work as everyone else's.

lines.frame: I asked the man who keeps the shift list how the first week had gone. He read out what was written:

lines.text: Heart is what runs out first around here. Before the food, before the stone.
I slept badly. It wasn't noise. It was there being no noise at all.
I ran my hand over what you laid yesterday. It's solid. That kept me in a good mood until nearly midday.
My uncle stopped coming. Said he's lost a house once already and won't sit here waiting to lose another. I didn't argue with him.

choices.text: I brought you stone. Take it.

lines.text: Stone? For me?
My piece is the shortest on the street and I'm behind on it anyway. I wasn't going to ask anyone.
I'll remember this. That's not a turn of phrase, it's a warning: I remember.
Today I split my daughters up. One on the stone, the other up there watching the road. I didn't like either decision.
If you left people on watch last night, you've seen what came of it. If you didn't, you've seen that too.
I'm not going to tell you what to do. Only that the arithmetic doesn't change, and the wall doesn't know how many hands you have.
It was on my stretch. Woke up to one stone out of place. Just the one, in the middle, picked on purpose.
That's not damage, it's a message. Nobody who wants a wall down moves a single stone.
They don't want to come in. They want us to stop on our own and leave saying we tried.
Meremoth. I work the stretch up on the rise, near the old gate.
Don't mind the face. I slept badly. The road makes noise at night and I hear all of it from here.
It's probably nothing. It's always nothing.
Meremoth. I went out for lime on the low road before the sun was up.
I saw riders. Four, maybe five. They stopped at the bend, the far side of the stream, and stood looking this way for longer than anyone looks at nothing.
They didn't come down. They went back the same way, in no hurry.
I'm telling you because I don't know what to do with it. You're the one who decides where your people are tonight.

choices.text: You are awake at night. Did you hear anything else this week?
I'll think about what to do with that.

lines.text: Zaccur. I'm from here, born three streets from all this rubble.
I've seen a wall come down and I've seen people promise to put one up. You're the first who turned up with stone in your hands.
That counts for something. I don't know how much yet.
Zaccur. My brother-in-law drives cattle the other side of the valley and comes down the low road every day, without fail.
Nobody's coming. If troops were moving, the cattle would scatter and he'd see the dust a long way off. There hasn't been any dust this week.
Half this city hasn't slept properly since the man from the capital turned up. Sees a rider in every shadow and hears a drum in every gust of wind.
I sleep. And I wake early, and I lay more stone than the ones who stayed up. Do your own arithmetic.
Malchijah. I run Beth Haccherem, a whole district, and not one yard of wall.
I came because I was told to come. I'm staying because I looked at the size of the hole.
If a letter comes for you, it goes through my hands first. That's the only useful job I have here.
Malchijah, of Beth Haccherem. I run a district with no wall on it at all today, so don't ask me for building advice.
This came for you. Three men, on horseback, left it and rode off without dismounting.
They want to talk. At a village out on the plain, a day's walk from here. They say it's about an arrangement that suits both sides.
It might be a real conversation. It might be that they only want you a day away from here. I read the same letter you did and I can't tell you which.
And know the price before you answer: going down eats the whole day's work. Whatever is half-laid on the open stretch will not survive your absence.
And I'm not going in your place.

choices.text: I'll go down. I want to hear what they have.
I'm not going down. I have stone to lay.
I don't know yet. I'll answer later.

lines.text: You answered that you're not going down. They'll send again. People like that send four times before they change tactics.

lines.frame: They called the man from the capital down the same way. His answer was set down like this:

lines.text: Get back to the wall. The stone doesn't lay itself.
You're going. All right. I'll tell the ones who are staying.
A day on the road, and a day without you up here. Somebody covers your stretch, and nobody covers someone else's stretch the way they cover their own.
If they say anything worth hearing, tell me when you're back. I mean it: I want to know.
You're back. Were they polite?
They always are. They offered one thing you could write down and one you couldn't. You're the one who knows which is worth what.
A day is a day. Tomorrow we'll see what it cost.
The well in the square is deep and the water is dark. They say there have been fish in it since this place was an open cistern.
The line goes down. The line comes up. Nothing comes with it.
Nothing again. One of Shallum's daughters walks past, looks into the well, looks at you, and carries on.
The water doesn't move.
The girl comes back. Points at the other side of the well, says nothing, and goes.
You cast on the other side. On the third try the fish come up, and more of them than you can hold.

lines.frame: Somewhere else, it was set down like this:

lines.text: Timber came into the square. Proper timber, whole beams. You don't get that out of rubble, out of rubble you get gravel.
Stone and timber make a block, and a block goes up faster than loose stone. My father said the same about resin: put two weak things together and you get one that works.
There's material spare now and people short. It's the first good complaint I've made on this street.
My two are measuring the stretch with a cord. When they've finished I'll tell you how much is really left, not how much it looks like.
People came down the low road early. They didn't come up. They just laughed, loud enough to carry this far.
They asked whether we were going to raise this in a day. They asked whether burnt stone goes back to being stone.

lines.frame: The man from the capital answered before I had thought of an answer. It was set down like this:

lines.text: I wouldn't have put it that way. But it was said, and they left without waiting for the second half.
There were five. I counted four and told you four. It was five.
I'm not apologising for counting wrong. I'm telling you that I saw them, and that I still see them.
My brother-in-law didn't come down the low road yesterday. I found out this morning, too late to be any use.
I didn't invent anything. I repeated something I hadn't checked, and I repeated it with a great deal of certainty. I think that's worse.
If you listened to me, that's not on you.
The timber was not bought here. It was asked for by letter, long before any of us picked up a stone.

lines.frame: Asked of a man who looks after the king's woodland. The request was recorded with a name on it and a purpose:

lines.text: It's the only thing on this job that didn't come out of the ground here. Everything else we scavenge, break and lay.
Keep that in mind: not every door opens with a stone in your hand. Some open with paper, and paper takes months.
I'll be around here. Somebody has to tell you where the quarry is when you ask.
Get the rubble first. Without stone, the rest is talk.
Everyone took a stretch. I took the one in front of my house, like he said.
He's still up on the stone. Answers one person at a time, without raising his voice, and points at different stretches of the wall.
Nobody introduced you to him and you won't get near him now.
I did. And I kept that one to myself, because at the time it didn't seem worth telling.
His first night here a horse went down the lower street, slow, on its own. I took it for a thief and stayed quiet.

lines.frame: I only understood when he spoke in the square. He said himself that he told nobody before he went:

lines.text: He went towards the valley, along the bottom, where the rubble closes in and no animal gets through. On foot for the rest of it, I'd guess.

lines.frame: He said as well what he went to look at, and how far he got:

lines.text: He was back before first light and spent the next day saying nothing. He only opened his mouth once he knew the size of it on his own feet.
I tell you and nobody else. You do the same thing: look first, give the order after.
The square was full at first light. Today isn't a working day: it's the day the work gets divided, and nobody wants to arrive after the dividing.
The man from the capital has a list in his hand and a scribe beside him. This is not a speech. It is a roll call.

lines.frame: He starts at the north gate, the sheep gate, with the ones who were already there before anybody gave an order. It was set down like this:

lines.text: — This stretch already has its people. The next ones go to whoever puts a hand up.

lines.frame: The men of Jericho come in next to them, and after them Zaccur son of Imri, who you have already met. The list goes on in the same tone, without one adjective:

lines.text: — If you live here, you take the piece in front of your own house. If you came in from outside, you take what is beside it.
A goldsmith puts himself forward. A perfumer behind him. Neither of them works in stone and neither of them is here by mistake.

lines.frame: The two go into the list under the trade they have, not the one they are doing today:

lines.text: Shallum puts a hand up and says his daughters lay with him. Nobody laughs and nobody argues.

lines.frame: It was written down with the daughters in it, and that is not a common thing to find written down:

lines.text: The men of one town come forward and take their stretch. The leading men of that same town stay behind them and do not put a hand up. The scribe records both.

lines.frame: He recorded it the way it happened:

lines.text: After that he reads out the four stretches left on this end of the city, one at a time, saying each one aloud so it is clear which is which.
— Whoever takes a stretch answers for it. That isn't a punishment.
The scribe doesn't look up. He writes it down so that when it is standing, it is known whose hands did it.
The square breaks up on its own. Everyone walks off towards the piece that is theirs now.
A perfumer took a stretch today. A perfumer. I laughed, and then I was ashamed of having laughed.
My father would have taken one too. He never raised anything in his life, but he never let anything fall on its own either.
Today is the lightest day we're going to get. Make the most of it and talk to everyone. Tomorrow nobody has the time.
It's on the record: my two with me. I didn't ask for it to be put down and it was put down.
Twenty years laying stone and it's the first time anyone has written down who did it, and not just what was done.
Today won't produce much. Today is for people to look around and see how many of them there are. That counts, and it counts tomorrow.
I counted the stretches on this end: four. Mine is the second, the one facing the open ground.
I knew already. It's just that today it was said in front of everyone, and it's a different thing once it's said.
Rest today. That isn't lazy advice: the ones who don't rest before they start are the ones who stop halfway.
Nobody is watching the road today. They're all looking inwards, at the list.
I'll watch anyway. It isn't suspicion. It's habit, and it costs little.
If I see anything you're the first to know. As always, without my knowing whether it's nothing.
My name came out near the top of the list, next to the men of Jericho. That's no credit to me: it's the order of who lived here first.
I got it wrong with you the other day. I took a stretch so I wouldn't only be the one who talks.
If I tell you one more thing I haven't seen, you have the right to laugh at me in front of the others.
The whole of Beth Haccherem is written down under my name. One district, one stretch, and eleven men who are not obliged to be here.
Today I'm not handling letters. Today I'm counting people, which is my real job.
Count as well. It's the only number in this city that is going up this week.
They stop on the upper road, where the wind carries a voice into the city. Where they can be seen and not reached.

lines.frame: The one up there is the man from Samaria. Word of the work reached him before we had laid the first course, and what that did to him was set down:
Then he spoke, in front of his brothers and the army of Samaria. What he said was written down whole:

lines.text: — Are you listening? You're meant to. I don't need anything more than this: I talk, and you stop on your own.

lines.frame: What he wants out of it is no secret, and it is not our guess: it was written down, in those words.
The Ammonite is beside him. He adds a short joke, and the joke was written down too:

lines.text: On this side nobody answers. There is nobody to answer: they are too far off to hear and too close to ignore.
There is nothing to be done about it today except lay stone in front of them until they tire of talking to themselves.

lines.frame: That is what was done, and what was done fitted into a single line:

lines.text: You can hear it from here. You can't make out all of it, which is worse: we fill in the rest ourselves, and we fill it in badly.
I laid nine stones today counting out loud, just so I was not counting what they were saying.
There's no split that helps with this. It isn't an attack. There is no guard against a joke.
My youngest asked whether they're right. I said I don't know, and that we raise it anyway.
I'm on the stretch that faces them. I hear it first hand and I don't pass it on, because passing it on is their job, not mine.
Bring stone and stand next to me for an hour. Two people saying nothing together goes further than one saying nothing alone.

choices.text: Come up with me. I want to hear what they're shouting.
I don't want to hear it. Hand me a stone.

lines.text: Two men off my block didn't come today. It wasn't fear of an army. It was shame at standing next to something people are laughing at.
That is exactly what they want, and it's free for them. Shouting from a distance costs nothing.
They aren't alone today. The upper road is full, and they're coming in from four sides.

lines.frame: Samaria, the Ammonites, the Arabs and the men of Ashdod heard that the gaps were closing. What that stirred in them was recorded:
And what they agreed among themselves was recorded too, all of them at once:

lines.text: — Last time I only talked, and you carried on. Today I brought the ones who do not talk.
He doesn't come forward. He stays where the whole city can see him, which is where he has always been.

choices.text: Look at who else came down with him.

lines.text: The Ammonite comes a little lower than the rest. He knows this road: he has family married in here, and people up there who answer his letters.

lines.frame: What the ones outside were saying among themselves came in through the people who live near them, and it came in ten times over:

lines.text: — You have too many people on the wall and too few at home. One of the two is open right now, and I have all day to find out which.
Nobody on this side answers. One man on this side comes down off the wall and goes home, and that was the point.
I counted wrong once and you listened to me anyway. I am counting again: there are a lot of them, and they are from different places.
People from different places don't fight side by side for long. Only today they are still in one piece.
The ones who live near them came in ten times today to warn us. Ten times the same sentence, with more fear inside it each time.
I haven't sent anyone home. Let one go and the whole line goes, and I'd have no way of calling them back.
This is it. I said it would be my stretch and it isn't: it's all of them at once, and that is what they want us to feel.
Choose where you stand. There's no choosing again halfway through.

choices.text: I'll stay on my stretch. Get to yours.

lines.text: Morning came and nobody with it. The upper road is as empty today as it was full yesterday.
The city did not relax because of that. It did two things on the same day, and both of them ended up in the same sentence.

lines.frame: One sentence with an "and" in the middle. The "and" is the whole sentence:

lines.text: Both, by the same people, on the same day. Neither instead of the other, and neither because the other failed.

lines.frame: When the fear tightened, what was said to the people was set down like this:

lines.text: Nobody told anyone to be brave. They were told to remember who sleeps on the inside.

lines.frame: And the day's arithmetic was written down. It is a simple division, and the most expensive this city has ever made:

lines.text: From here on it is like this every day. It produces less. It's the only way that doesn't stop.

lines.frame: They agreed on a signal as well, because the city is too long for shouting. Wherever the trumpet sounds, that is where everyone runs:

lines.text: Today I worked with one hand and held something I don't know how to use in the other.
It produces less. It produces. It's the first time in a week I haven't had to choose between the two.
The arithmetic has changed. It's not who goes up and who lays any more: it's each person doing both, and neither of the two going to zero.
I argued against it all week. I was wrong, and I'm saying so out loud so I don't have to say it twice.

choices.text: Show me the whole day's arithmetic.
I'll look later. I have a course to close.

lines.text: They agreed a signal on the trumpet. Wherever it sounds, everyone drops what they are doing and runs there.
It's the first thing since I got here that works for people spread out. Until today all we had was shouting, and shouting doesn't turn a corner.
My eleven are split: six on the stone, five up top. Tomorrow it swaps, so nobody gets good at only one of the two.
And not a single letter came today. That worries me more than when one does.
Four came. Four times the same letter, with the same village on the plain and the same day named in it.

lines.frame: The first one asked for the meeting like this, and the other three repeated it without moving a comma:
This invitation has been made once already, and the answer given at the time was recorded. It has not changed since:

lines.text: And a fifth came, open, with no seal on it. Open on purpose: so that everybody reads it on the way before it reaches you.

lines.frame: That fifth one accuses the work of something else, and says outright what it wants the accusation to achieve:

lines.text: I read all five. Not one of them is about a wall. All of them are about you.

choices.text: Read the fifth one aloud. I want it the way the city got it.
Keep all five. I will read them after sundown.

lines.text: The open letter went round the city before it reached your hand. Half the work stopped to listen to somebody read it aloud.
Nobody is coming up the road today. What is coming is paper, and paper gets in over any wall.
This is not answered with a guard. A guard is no use against a sentence that is already going round.
What is any use is checking what is written now against what was written before. It is the only thing that tells a true letter from a well-made one.

choices.text: See who signs it at the bottom.

lines.text: The fifth letter has his name at the bottom of it and no seal on the top.
— Come and talk. A day on the road, a village, an afternoon. That is all.
— I've asked four times with the letter closed. This one I left open, and you'll understand why before the day is out.
— Name the day. I can wait. I have always waited.
Look at the wall. End to end, now, before anyone tells you what to look at.

lines.frame: When there was no gap left in it, and before the doors were hung, it was written down like this:

lines.text: The doors are missing. That's all. A city with no doors isn't a city yet, but it isn't rubble any more.
I asked the scribe how many days it took, first to last. He counted twice before he answered.

lines.frame: He read the count out the way it was written, with the day and the month it closed on:

lines.text: Fifty-two. It took me longer than that to redo my own kitchen, and the kitchen had nobody shouting at it from outside.

lines.frame: And it was written down what the ones outside felt when they heard the count:

lines.text: I read the open letter. It's well written, and that's the problem: badly made things we throw out on our own.
Check it against what was written before. If it matches, it's true. If it doesn't, it's only well made.
I was going to repeat it. I picked the letter up, opened my mouth, and remembered my brother-in-law and the low road.
I didn't repeat it. It's the first thing I've done properly in this city.
The door arrived in two leaves of timber, four men under each. Nobody spoke while they were going up.
Bars, bolts, and the sound a door makes the first time it closes. Half the city heard it from a distance and stopped what they were doing.

lines.frame: For the day the wall was to be handed over, they sent for the ones who can sing, from every village around. It was recorded like this:

lines.text: They came. They came from places nobody here visits, and they came on foot, with an instrument on their back.

lines.frame: Then they all went up onto the wall and split into two companies, which set off in opposite directions:

lines.text: One company went right. The other went left. The two halves went out of sight, one to each side of the city.
You stay where you are. Your stretch is the one that closes the circle, and it is over your stretch that the two halves meet again.

lines.frame: When they met, you could hear it a long way off. It was set down how far it carried:

lines.text: Afterwards somebody comes up with a shard of clay and a nail and writes on the stone of your stretch who repaired this piece.

lines.frame: It is what was done with the first door of this city, the north one, the sheep gate, and with the name of whoever raised it:

lines.text: It isn't a tribute. It's a record. In a hundred years somebody reads it and knows there were people here.
My sister comes back tomorrow. She sent to ask whether there is a door. I sent back that there is, and I sent it twice.
It's the stupidest thing to get emotional about. I got emotional anyway.
My two laid the last course of our stretch. I stood and watched and corrected nothing.
Twenty years. It isn't the biggest wall I've raised. It's the only one with the name of who raised it written on it.
The open ground is still there. The difference is that now it is on the outside of something.
Remember the first day, when I said there was room on my side? There still is. Come back whenever you like.
I go back to Beth Haccherem in the morning, with the eleven, and not one of the eleven wants to go.
I will take the news as it is: it worked, and it worked slowly.
The low road is clear. I went down it twice and saw no sign of anything.
All the noise is from up top, off the ridge. I prefer noise from up top: noise from up top I can see the source of.
No letters today, not for you and not for me. My eleven are all on the stone and I have nothing to send on.
So I carried stone. First time in twenty years. Tomorrow I will not be able to lift my arm, and it was worth it.
On my stretch the arithmetic is worse than average: facing open ground, it needs more people up top and leaves fewer for the stone.
I'm not going to ask to borrow anyone. I'll produce less, and I won't pretend I'm not producing less.
I haven't looked at the road once today. Not once. I noticed when the sun was already high.
It isn't that the danger is over. It's that today there is a door, and a door is the first thing since I got here that watches while I sleep.
